The British prime minister will make the case for a closer relationship with the EU in a House of Commons statement Monday.

AI generated Text-to-speech

LONDON — Andy Burnham will argue Monday it would be a “dereliction of duty” for Britain not to seek closer ties with the EU.

In a House of Commons statement reopening Britain's highly-charged Brexit debate, the prime minister will claim the vast majority of the public would back a closer relationship with the EU if it helps to control immigration and boost economic growth, according to a U.K. official briefed on the statement.

“Andy understands why some politicians don’t want to face up to the reality that Brexit has not delivered what they once promised. But it is time for a different conversation about what our long-term relationship should be,” said the U.K. official, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record.

“Sticking with the status quo and not working relentlessly to secure a good deal that boosts growth would be a major dereliction of duty.”

At Labour's annual conference last month, Burnham said Britain's departure from the bloc had done “more harm than good” and he pledged to use the imminent U.K.-EU summit — due to take place next month — to put forward “what I believe the different options are for Britain's long-term relationship with our European partners.”

In subsequent interviews, he said it's possible a future Labour manifesto could include a pledge to hold an “in-out” referendum on rejoining the EU.

The U.K. prime minister will address MPs after telling the Rest is Politics podcast it is “clear” Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum.

“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: ‘Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia?’ And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” Burnham said.

In subsequent media interviews Monday, Foreign Office Minister Stephen Doughty suggested that the U.K. government does not believe that interference was successful.

“Russia has attempted to interfere in a number of our democratic processes over a sustained period,” Doughty told LBC Monday, but he added: “They haven't succeeded in their many, many attempts to undermine our processes.”

Pushed in a Sky News interview about whether the Brexit referendum result is unsafe, Doughty said “the result is the result.”

Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage, one of the most high profile campaigners for Brexit in 2016, said Burnham's Russian interference claim was "outrageous."

“There was no Russian interference, and the Russia hoax has run all the way through this," he said. “This is out of touch, out of date Andy Burnham, with all sorts of bizarre ideas."

Dan Bloom contributed reporting.

This story has been updated to include comments from Nigel Farage.
